purpose: Amantadine is used to help manage symptoms of Parkinson's disease, such as stiffness, tremors, and trouble moving. It can also help reduce involuntary movements (called dyskinesia) that can happen as a side effect of Parkinson's medications. In the past, it was also used to prevent and treat certain types of flu, though this use is now less common.
how_it_works: Amantadine works in the brain by boosting the activity of a chemical called dopamine, which helps control smooth, coordinated movement. It also blocks certain brain receptors (called NMDA receptors) that, when overactive, can cause those unwanted jerky or writhing movements. Think of it as helping to rebalance the signals your brain sends to your muscles.
common_side_effects: You might notice dizziness, trouble sleeping, or feeling confused or lightheaded, especially when you first start taking it. Some people get nausea, dry mouth, or constipation. A blotchy purplish skin discoloration on the legs (called livedo reticularis) can also happen but is harmless and usually goes away when you stop the medication. Swelling in the ankles or feet is also fairly common.
warnings: Do not stop taking amantadine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious problems, especially for Parkinson's patients. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, because the dose may need to be adjusted. This medication can cause dizziness or confusion, so be careful when driving or operating machinery. Some people experience hallucinations or mood changes, so let your doctor know right away if you notice anything unusual with your thinking or behavior. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on what condition is being treated and which form of the medication you are taking. For Parkinson's symptoms, a common starting dose of regular (immediate-release) tablets is 100 mg once or twice a day. Extended-release forms like Gocovri are taken once at bedtime, usually starting at 137 mg and possibly increased to 274 mg. Your doctor will find the right dose for you, and it may be lower if you have kidney problems. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
